questions.problem: The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by $v(t)=(t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+4t).$ Calculate the velocity of the particle when the acceleration $a$ is equal to $6\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+4t) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1+4 \\  & =5+\operatorname{ln}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=6,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =5+\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =1 \\ {e}^{(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)} & ={e}^{1} \\ t & =e\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=e,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(e) & =(e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+4e) \\  & =e(1)+4e \\  & =5e\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=6\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $5e\text{ m/s}.$

questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by $v(t)=\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7}.$ Calculate the velocity of the particle when the acceleration $a$ is equal to $\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

When $a=\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ the velocity is $v=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7}) \\  & =\frac{2t+1}{2\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=\frac{1}{2},$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{2t+1}{2\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7}} \\ 1 & =\frac{2t+1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7}} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7} & =2t+1 \\ {(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+t+7})}^{2} & ={(2t+1)}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+t+7 & =4{t}^{2}+4t+1 \\ 0 & =3{t}^{2}+3t-6 \\ 0 & ={t}^{2}+t-2 \\ 0 & =(t-1)(t+2) \\ t & =1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $t=1$ since $t\ge 0.$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=1,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =\sqrt{(1)^{2}+1+7} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+7} \\  & =3\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=\frac{1}{2}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $v=3\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem: The velocity $v$ (in $\text{m/s}$) of a particle at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by $v(t)=4{t}^{2}-16t+15.$ Calculate the velocity of the particle when the acceleration $a$ is equal to $0\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2}-16t+15) \\  & =8t-16\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=0,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8t-16 \\ 8t & =16 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, to calculate the velocity at time $t=2,$ we substitute this into the equation for the velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =4(2)^{2}-16(2)+15 \\  & =16-32+15 \\  & =-1\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity when $a=0\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is $-1\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)=4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2},$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Find the time when the particle's acceleration is equal to $a=70\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

The acceleration is $70\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ at
$t=$
{{field-1}} seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}) \\  & =12{t}^{2}-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12{t}^{2}-2t) \\  & =24t-2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the time when the acceleration is $a=70,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}70 & =24t-2 \\ 24t & =72 \\ t & =3\text{ }\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration is $70\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}$ at $t=3$ seconds.

questions.problem: The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)=4{t}^{3}+10{t}^{2}-15$, where $t$ is measured in seconds.  Find the particle's acceleration at $t=3$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}+10{t}^{2}-15) \\  & =12{t}^{2}+20t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12{t}^{2}+20t) \\  & =24t+20\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=3$, we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(3) & =24(3)+20 \\  & =72+20 \\  & =92\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=3$ seconds is $92\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
The displacement (in meters) of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)=2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}+3t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds. Find the particle's acceleration at $t=\frac{1}{2}$ second.

$a(\frac{1}{2})=$
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-{t}^{2}+3t) \\  & =8{t}^{3}-2t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{3}-2t+3) \\  & =24{t}^{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=\frac{1}{2}$ second, we substitute $t=\frac{1}{2}$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(\frac{1}{2}) & =24{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-2 \\  & =24\cdot \frac{1}{4}-2 \\  & =4\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: The position $x$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by $x(t) = 1+2t+3t^2+4t^3$. Calculate the acceleration of the particle at time $t=0$.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $x(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t+3{t}^{2}+4{t}^{3}) \\  & =2+6t+12{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+6t+12{t}^{2}) \\  & =6+24t.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=0$, we substitute this into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(0) & =6+24(0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=0$ is $6$.
